newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds enters 1950s papers at Florida trial.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds enters 1950s papers at Florida trial.

text.p: R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. presented four-decade-old newspaper articles and health reports at a wrongful death trial Wednesday in an apparent attempt to show that medical experts of that era were uncertain about a link between smoking and cancer.

Reynolds attorney Paul Crist introduced into evidence a series of papers, including a 1954 New York Times article, medical journal stories and a 1962 public health study that questioned whether smoking caused cancer.
The papers were entered during the fifth day of testimony of Dr. Allan Feingold, a Miami physician appearing as an expert witness for plaintiff Dana Raulerson.
Raulerson has sued the tobacco company on behalf of the estate of her sister, Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.
Raulerson's lawsuit alleges that Reynolds manufactured a dangerous product and failed to fix it.

The New York Times article, reporting on a San Francisco meeting of the American College of Chest Physicians, was headlined "Chest Physicians Bar Linking of Cigarettes to Cancer" and quoted doctors who disputed the claim that smoking was linked to lung cancer.

Feingold had testified Tuesday that Reynolds officials "definitely knew" in the 1950s that smoking caused lung cancer, noting studies that drew parallels between a rise in cigarette smoking and an increasing incidence of lung cancer in the first half of the century.
Asked by Crist why some physicians in the 1950s did not concur with that theory, Feingold said: "There were people who disputed the obvious."
Crist also presented a 1962 report by Lewis Robbins, identified as a senior public health official for the U.S. government.

The report said there was no conclusive evidence that smoking caused cancer and indicated researchers were looking at other possible causes, including car exhaust and other air pollution, for a rise in lung cancer rates.
"For the medical investigator ... the evidence still does not add up to conclusive proof that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer," Robbins wrote.
As cross-examination continued Wednesday, Crist continued his efforts to discredit Feingold's earlier testimony that smoking causes cancer and nicotine is addictive.

Feingold was expected to complete his testimony late Wednesday. The next expert witness for the plaintiff is expected to be Victor Roggli, a Duke University pathologist who was expected to testify about the origin and location of Connor's fatal cancer.
R.J. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
